r: Sleep loss harms memory at both ends of the process. In Matthew Walker's group, one sleepless night cut the hippocampus's ability to encode new information by roughly 40%, as if its inbox were full and could take no more. The deeper damage happens while we sleep. During slow-wave sleep, 0.5–1 Hz oscillations occur alongside 11–16 Hz spindles and hippocampal sharp-wave ripples. Together they replay the day's memory traces and send them to the neocortex for long-term storage. Without that night shift, consolidation stalls. Researchers also suspect that the brain's glymphatic system, which clears waste, falls behind. In mice, its interstitial channels widen by about 60% during sleep. Without that clearing, metabolic debris such as amyloid-beta may cloud the next day's learning. Even partial restriction adds up. Subjects limited to six hours for two weeks did as poorly on attention tests as people who were fully sleep-deprived, yet they rated themselves as only mildly impaired. In short, memory is built by day but banked by night.
